meta.description: Guide-only natural-history profiles for evidence-backed Northern Virginia fish-community records. These profiles enrich the Fish Guide but are deliberately excluded from opportunity scoring.
meta.provenance: Reviewed against U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, U.S. Geological Survey, National Park Service, Fairfax County, and state fisheries-agency references.

profiles.statusNote: A native catadromous fish: it grows in rivers and estuaries, then migrates to the Sargasso Sea to spawn.
profiles.identification: A long, snake-like fish with a continuous dorsal, tail, and anal fin, a protruding lower jaw, and tiny scales hidden beneath a thick mucus layer. Unlike a lamprey, it has a true jaw and paired pectoral fins.
profiles.diet: A night-feeding predator and scavenger that eats crustaceans, aquatic insects, worms, and fish; larger eels take larger prey.
profiles.handlingNote: Wet your hands before handling its mucus-coated skin and check the water-specific consumption advisory before considering harvest.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Fish after dark with a simple bottom rig around rock, wood, bridge cover, and connected river channels; keep the bait close to the bottom.

profiles.notes: This biology profile does not create a BiteMap opportunity score. Eel abundance and migration access can change sharply above dams and other barriers.

profiles.statusNote: Native and widespread in Northern Virginia headwaters; Fairfax County describes it as the county's most commonly collected fish.
profiles.identification: A small, stout minnow with a dark stripe running from the tail through the eye and around the downturned snout. Adults have olive backs and pale bellies; breeding males may show rusty orange along the sides and fin bases.
profiles.diet: Aquatic and terrestrial insects, fish and invertebrate eggs, diatoms and other algae, plant material, and detritus.
profiles.handlingNote: A small native forage fish rather than a normal hook-and-line target; release incidental captures promptly and do not move baitfish between waters.

confusedWith.tell: Blacknose dace has a bold eye-to-tail stripe and a shorter snout; longnose dace has a distinctly overhanging snout, small barbels, and a mottled pattern.

profiles.notes: Presence is informative about the stream community, not an angling forecast. A dace-heavy sample with few other species can also occur in degraded habitat.

profiles.statusNote: A native, highly tolerant bullhead of warm, slow water and soft bottoms.
profiles.identification: A compact, mottled brown catfish with dark chin barbels and a square or only slightly notched tail. The dark chin whiskers separate it from the pale-whiskered yellow bullhead.
profiles.diet: An omnivorous bottom feeder taking aquatic insects, worms, crayfish, mollusks, small fish, algae, and other plant material.
profiles.handlingNote: The dorsal and pectoral spines can puncture a hand. Grip behind the spines and verify local consumption advice before harvest.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Still-fish a bottom rig around soft-bottom coves, vegetation edges, and slow pools, especially on summer evenings and after dark.

confusedWith.tell: Brown bullhead has dark chin barbels and usually stronger mottling; yellow bullhead has white or yellow chin barbels.

profiles.notes: Brown bullhead tolerates warmth, low oxygen, and turbidity better than many fishes, so presence alone is not evidence of high water quality.

profiles.statusNote: A common native headwater minnow and important prey fish in small streams.
profiles.identification: A robust minnow with a dark spot at the front base of the dorsal fin, another spot at the tail base, and a large mouth. Young fish show a dark lateral stripe; adults may have a tiny barbel at the corner of the mouth.
profiles.diet: Mostly aquatic and terrestrial insects, with larger fish also eating crayfish, worms, mollusks, and small fish.
profiles.handlingNote: Do not transfer creek chubs between drainages as bait; bait-bucket release can spread fish and disease beyond their native water.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.cool: Use tiny spinners, wet flies, or a small worm in pools below riffles and around root cover.
primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Fish shaded headwater pools and slower runs near sunset with ultralight tackle.

confusedWith.tell: Creek chub has a distinct dark spot at the front of the dorsal-fin base; fallfish lacks that spot and adults show dark-edged scales.

profiles.notes: This is a guide profile only. Its sunset activity and small-stream tactics are descriptive and do not feed the BiteMap score.

profiles.statusNote: A large native minnow of the Potomac drainage and one of the region's most underrated ultralight sport fish.
profiles.identification: A silvery to brassy, chub-shaped fish with a large mouth, dark-edged scales on adults, and no black spot at the front of the dorsal fin. A small fleshy barbel may sit in the groove behind the upper jaw.
profiles.diet: Young fish eat algae and aquatic or terrestrial insects; larger fallfish add crayfish, fish, and seasonally abundant fish eggs.
profiles.handlingNote: Treat large fallfish as a native sport fish: wet your hands, support the body, and release quickly if not keeping them under current rules.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.cool: Cast small spinners, spoons, nymphs, or streamers across current seams and the tails of pools.
primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Work deeper runs, boulder edges, and shaded pools with ultralight lures or a lightly weighted worm.

confusedWith.tell: Fallfish lacks the creek chub's black dorsal-base spot and grows larger; adult fallfish often have conspicuously dark-edged scales.

profiles.notes: Fallfish are catchable, but this entry remains guide-only until BiteMap has a reviewed temperature and seasonal scoring profile.

profiles.statusNote: Native farther west in North America but introduced and established in much of Atlantic-slope Virginia, including Northern Virginia waters.
profiles.identification: A thick-bodied sunfish with a comparatively large mouth, blue-green cheek streaks, a long dark ear flap, and yellow to orange edging on the dorsal, tail, and anal fins.
profiles.diet: A visual predator that eats insects, crayfish, and small fish.
profiles.handlingNote: Its sharp dorsal spines can catch skin or fabric. Fold the spines flat before handling and never release live fish into another waterbody.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Fish daylight hours around wood, undercut banks, vegetation, and quiet creek pools with a small worm under a float or an ultralight lure.

confusedWith.tell: Green sunfish has a much larger mouth, a longer body, and yellow-orange fin margins; bluegill is deeper-bodied with a small mouth and solid dark ear flap.
Pumpkinseed has a small mouth and a red-orange crescent on the ear flap; green sunfish has a large mouth and pale fin edges.

profiles.notes: The 70 F spawning threshold comes from the Missouri Department of Conservation and is a broad biological cue, not a local bite trigger.

profiles.statusNote: A native riffle specialist of cool, fast, rocky streams.
profiles.identification: A slender, mottled dace with a long snout that overhangs the small mouth, tiny scales, and a small barbel at each corner of the mouth. Breeding fish can show red around the mouth and fin bases.
profiles.diet: A bottom feeder taking mayfly, blackfly, and midge larvae, other small invertebrates, and some algae.
profiles.handlingNote: A small native forage fish and stream-community indicator, not a normal angling target. Return incidental captures to the same water promptly.

confusedWith.tell: Longnose dace has an overhanging snout, barbels, and mottling; blacknose dace has a bold dark stripe through the eye and a shorter snout.

profiles.notes: Riffle habitat and clean interstitial spaces matter more than a simple waterbody label for this species.

profiles.statusNote: A native coldwater bottom fish associated with spring-fed streams and rocky cover.
profiles.identification: A scaleless, mottled brown bottom fish with a broad flattened head, very large fan-shaped pectoral fins, and two dorsal fins. Its color can shift to match the streambed.
profiles.diet: A benthic ambush predator eating aquatic insect larvae, crustaceans, worms, occasional small fish, and sometimes other sculpins.
profiles.handlingNote: Sculpins are small native predators and useful coldwater indicators. Avoid disturbing the rocks and submerged cover they use for shelter and nests.

confusedWith.tell: Sculpins have a much broader head, huge pectoral fins, and no scales; tessellated darters are slender, scaled, and marked with small W- or X-shaped blotches.

profiles.notes: Taxonomy within the mottled-sculpin complex has changed in parts of North America; BiteMap uses the community-record name supplied by its regional evidence.

profiles.statusNote: A native, clear-stream bottom feeder often associated with healthy gravel and rubble habitat.
profiles.identification: A stout sucker with a large, blocky head, a concave profile behind the eyes, broad fleshy lips beneath the snout, and dark saddle-like bands across a mottled body.
profiles.diet: Uses its fleshy lips and head to turn stones and vacuum up immature aquatic insects and other small bottom organisms.
profiles.handlingNote: Northern hogsuckers are native ecosystem engineers: feeding exposes insects that other fish follow and eat. Release incidental captures carefully.

confusedWith.tell: Northern hogsucker has a larger, blockier head and dark saddles; white sucker is more cylindrical and usually plain brown to olive.

profiles.notes: This species is seldom caught on a baited hook. Its guide entry emphasizes identification and ecological role rather than lure advice.

profiles.statusNote: A colorful native sunfish of vegetated shallows, quiet rivers, ponds, and lakes.
profiles.identification: A deep, disk-shaped sunfish with blue-green wavy cheek lines, an orange belly, and a red-orange crescent on the rear of the dark ear flap. The mouth is noticeably smaller than a green sunfish's.
profiles.diet: Aquatic insects, snails, small clams and other crustaceans, plus occasional small fish; specialized crushing teeth help it eat snails.
profiles.handlingNote: Fold the sharp dorsal spines before handling. Wet hands and a quick release protect the fish's slime coat.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.cool: Look for warming, sheltered shallows and work a tiny jig, nymph, or worm slowly near cover.
primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Fish vegetation edges, docks, submerged wood, and shallow spawning colonies with a tiny bait under a float or a small fly.

confusedWith.tell: Pumpkinseed has blue cheek lines and a red-orange mark on the ear flap; bluegill has a solid dark ear flap and lacks the bright red crescent.
Pumpkinseed is deeper-bodied with a small mouth; green sunfish has a larger mouth and yellow-orange fin margins.

profiles.notes: Pumpkinseed commonly hybridize with other sunfish, so some individuals will not match every field mark cleanly.

profiles.statusNote: A native, structure-oriented sunfish of rocky rivers, streams, and clear-water shorelines.
profiles.identification: A stocky olive-to-brassy sunfish with rows of dark spots, a large mouth, and red to orange eyes. It has six anal-fin spines, compared with three on most other local sunfish.
profiles.diet: An opportunistic predator of crayfish, aquatic insects, and smaller fish, feeding heavily around dawn, dusk, and other low-light periods.
profiles.handlingNote: Support larger fish horizontally and watch the dorsal and anal spines when unhooking them.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.cool: Drift a small minnow, crayfish, grub, or hellgrammite along the bottom of rocky pools and current pockets.
primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Target boulders, ledges, rootwads, and water-willow edges early and late with small spinners, grubs, or live bait.

profiles.notes: Rock bass are genuinely catchable, but this profile remains outside the ranking model until its local condition-response evidence is reviewed.

profiles.statusNote: A native migratory river sucker and benthic feeder, often associated with flowing water and clean mineral substrate.
profiles.identification: A slender, coarse-scaled sucker with a short head, fleshy folded lips beneath the snout, a short dorsal fin, and often orange to red lower fins and tail.
profiles.diet: Primarily immature midges, mayflies, and caddisflies grubbed from sand, gravel, and rubble.
profiles.handlingNote: Redhorse are native, long-lived river fish that are often misidentified. Release unwanted fish carefully and never discard them as 'rough fish.'

confusedWith.tell: Shorthead redhorse has coarser scales, a shorter head, and often reddish lower fins; white sucker is plainer and has smaller scales toward the head.

profiles.notes: Spring tributary movements can concentrate fish, but the month shown is a broad biological window and not a harvest recommendation.

profiles.statusNote: A native Atlantic-slope darter that lives on the bottom of streams and rivers.
profiles.identification: A small sandy-tan bottom fish with a continuous lateral line and a row of roughly 9 to 11 dark W- or X-shaped marks along the sides. It rests propped on its pelvic fins, then moves in abrupt darts.
profiles.diet: Small aquatic insect larvae and other bottom-dwelling invertebrates picked from sand, rubble, mud, and vegetation.
profiles.handlingNote: A small native community fish rather than an angling target. Avoid disturbing rocks or logs used as spawning cover.

confusedWith.tell: Tessellated darter is slender and scaled with W-shaped side marks; mottled sculpin has a broad head, huge pectoral fins, and no scales.

profiles.notes: The entry focuses on identification and habitat because tessellated darter is not a hook-and-line target.

profiles.statusNote: A widespread native coolwater sucker found in streams, rivers, and some lakes.
profiles.identification: A cylindrical olive-brown to bronze fish with a pale belly, a blunt snout, and a horizontal fleshy sucker mouth beneath the head. The dorsal and tail fins are slate gray while the lower fins are paler.
profiles.diet: A generalist bottom feeder that selects immature aquatic insects, fish eggs, and other small invertebrates from sediment and debris.
profiles.handlingNote: Suckers are native food-web links, not trash fish. Check water-specific consumption advice and release unwanted fish promptly.

confusedWith.tell: White sucker is more cylindrical and plain; northern hogsucker has a much larger blocky head and dark saddle marks.
White sucker is generally plainer with less colorful fins; shorthead redhorse has coarse scales, a shorter head, and often reddish lower fins.

profiles.notes: The profile does not infer local abundance. White sucker can occur across a wide range of stream conditions.

profiles.statusNote: A native bullhead of soft-bottom pools, sluggish backwaters, ponds, and reservoirs.
profiles.identification: An olive to yellow-brown bullhead with white or yellow chin barbels and a rounded or nearly straight tail. The pale chin whiskers are the quickest separation from brown bullhead.
profiles.diet: Crayfish, mussels, aquatic insects, fish and fish eggs; adults also take snails, small crustaceans, and some plant material.
profiles.handlingNote: Avoid the sharp dorsal and pectoral spines. Keep the fish behind the spines while unhooking and check local consumption advisories before harvest.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Fish a small bottom rig near leaf packs, woody cover, and soft-bottom pools during the early evening or after dark.

confusedWith.tell: Yellow bullhead has pale white-to-yellow chin barbels; brown bullhead has dark chin barbels and usually mottled sides.

profiles.notes: Bullhead bites are strongly associated with low light and bottom-oriented presentation, but no BiteMap condition score is generated for this species.

profiles.statusNote: A native Atlantic-slope catfish that tolerates tidal fresh and brackish water better than most local catfishes.
profiles.identification: A compact catfish with a broad head, white chin barbels, a dark back over pale sides, and a tail that is rounded or only shallowly forked. Channel and blue catfish have much more deeply forked tails.
profiles.diet: Fish are favored, but white catfish also eat aquatic insect larvae, crustaceans, fish eggs, and aquatic plants.
profiles.handlingNote: The dorsal and pectoral spines can puncture skin. Check tidal-river consumption advisories before keeping a fish for the table.

primaryTechniquesBySeason.warm: Bottom-fish sluggish channels, tidal holes, backwaters, and mud-bottom pools with fresh bait; moving water around a tide change can reposition fish.

confusedWith.tell: White catfish has a broad head and a rounded to shallowly forked tail; channel catfish has a distinctly deep fork and usually scattered dark spots when young.
Blue catfish has a deeply forked tail and a long straight-edged anal fin; white catfish has a much shallower tail fork and a shorter, rounded anal fin.

profiles.notes: This is the most estuary-oriented of BiteMap's guide-only catfishes; do not transfer its habitat preference to inland ponds.

profiles.statusNote: A native schooling forage fish that connects plankton and detritus to bass, catfish, crappie, birds, and other predators.
profiles.identification: A deep, silvery, strongly compressed fish with a blunt snout, a small subterminal mouth, sharp belly scutes, and a long whip-like final dorsal ray. Young fish usually show a dark shoulder spot.
profiles.diet: Primarily a filter feeder on phytoplankton and zooplankton, with adults also processing algae, plant debris, and organic detritus in a muscular gizzard-like stomach.
profiles.handlingNote: Gizzard shad are primarily forage, rarely a hook-and-line target. Do not move live shad between waters; they can overpopulate and alter food webs outside their native range.
profiles.notes: Shad abundance strongly affects predator fisheries, but this guide record is not a direct baitfish-density measurement at any BiteMap access point.
